extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, administrators, investigators, decisionmakers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors for determining when unwelcome sex-based conduct rises to a hostile-environment Title IX violation and related procedural obligations for recipients of Federal financial assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe or pervasive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment sex-based harassment is conduct that is so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations adopt a 'severe or pervasive' standard (allowing conduct that is severe but not pervasive, or pervasive but not severe). The Department replaced the word 'sufficiently' with 'so' to emphasize the link to limiting or denying access. The standard aligns more closely with Title VII and prior OCR guidance and is intended to allow a prompt and effective response when a student experiences a hostile environment. Examples of pervasive conduct include repeated incidents that limit a student's ability to complete coursework at their typical level; a single stray remark generally will not meet the level of pervasiveness. The inquiry must be tied to whether the conduct limits or denies access to the education program or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective and objective offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwelcome sex-based conduct must be evaluated both subjectively (from the complainant's perspective) and objectively (whether the conduct is objectively offensive to a reasonable person in the complainant's position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department added the word 'offensive' to both the subjective and objective elements. Both elements are distinct and must be satisfied with sufficient evidence for a finding of hostile environment harassment. The objective standard is assessed from the perspective of a reasonable person in the complainant's position; the subjective element refers to the complainant's own perception. Subjective offensiveness must be supported by evidence and alone is insufficient to support a finding or discipline. The inclusion of subjective and objective elements is consistent with Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Davis, Oncale, Harris).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits or denies access/benefits requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct meets the 'severe or pervasive' threshold if it 'limits or denies' a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'limits or denies' is used (order changed to 'limits' then 'denies' for clarity). Complainants need not show a particular measurable harm (like lower grades); grades are not the only evidence of impact. The recipient must evaluate the impact based on all relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence. The analysis focuses on whether the harassment limits or denies access based on sex; animus is not a required element. The Department rejects narrowing the standard to only absolute exclusion from participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to be considered (non-exhaustive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exhaustive list of factors to consider in determining whether conduct creates a hostile environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors (similar to those in the 2020 preamble and prior guidance) include: the degree to which the conduct affected one or more students' education; the type, frequency, and duration of the conduct; the identity of and relationship between the alleged harasser and the subject(s); the number of individuals involved; the age and sex of the alleged harasser and the subject(s); the size of the school, location of incidents, and context in which they occurred; other incidents at the school; and incidents of gender-based but nonsexual harassment. The list is not exhaustive; the totality of the circumstances must be examined, and interpretations of Title VII may inform Title IX analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations must be fact-specific and made based on the totality of known circumstances and all relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples are for guidance only and do not replace a full fact-specific analysis. Recipients should consider the entire record and context rather than any single factor or example. The Department declines to opine on specific hypotheticals without full factual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: No affirmative tracking of speech required
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not required to directly or indirectly track speech for which no complaint was made or of which the Title IX Coordinator has not been notified to establish pervasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pervasiveness can be shown by conduct that is widespread, openly practiced, or well-known to students and staff (e.g., hallways, graffiti, harassment during supervised recess). Recipients may, however, assess a complaint considering related complaints or notifications received by the Title IX Coordinator. Recordkeeping obligations for complaints/notifications of speech-based harassment are the same as for other complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping obligations for complaints and notifications (§106.8(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's recordkeeping obligations for complaints and notifications alleging speech-based sex-based harassment should be treated the same as other complaints and notifications of sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department determined recipients should maintain records consistent with §106.8(f)(1) and (2) for speech-based harassment complaints/notifications. The Department is unpersuaded that this imposes an obligation to track all speech; recordkeeping applies to complaints/notifications received.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment and academic freedom considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must consider First Amendment protections and academic freedom when speech or expression are involved; nothing in the final regulations requires recipients to restrict rights protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that removing references to the 'primacy of the First Amendment' in prior amendments was not intended to reduce First Amendment protections. While the First Amendment may affect how a recipient responds, recipients retain other means to remedy a hostile environment and remain free to determine whether discipline is appropriate and what form it should take. The Department will not compel private recipients to abide by the U.S. Constitution (that would be outside its authority), but Title IX obligations are not obviated by a conflicting State law that governs speech not protected by the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, impartiality, and due process safeguards for Title IX personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX Coordinators, investigators, and decisionmakers must be trained to serve impartially and avoid prejudgment, conflicts of interest, and bias; recipients must provide equitable treatment and due process under the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations require training on impartiality (§106.8(d)(2)) and acting without bias (§106.45(b)(2)). Postsecondary institutions must offer appeals on the basis that the Title IX Coordinator, investigator, or decisionmaker had a conflict of interest or bias that would change the outcome (§106.46(i)(1)(iii)). Recipients' obligations in §§106.45 and, if applicable, 106.46 ensure respondents' due process rights are respected and investigations are evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animus not required for finding harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Animus (hostile intent based on sex) is not a required element of a harassment claim under the final regulations; the focus is on whether the conduct limits or denies access on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with Davis and prior OCR guidance, a harassment analysis centers on the impact of the conduct on access to education rather than proof of animus. The Department reiterates that the absence of animus does not preclude a finding of sex-based harassment if the 'limits or denies' standard is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and illustrative scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the preamble or NPRM are illustrative and not definitive—any determination requires a fuller, fact-specific analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department provides examples to demonstrate contexts in which harassment may arise but declines to opine categorically on particular hypotheticals; the totality of circumstances must be considered. The Department also clarified examples do not expand or narrow the legal standard beyond the written definition.
